video_title: When AI Builds Your Portfolio, Who Checks the Work? ft. Rob Carver | Systematic Investor | Ep. 427
gist: Rob Carver and host Niels review a November selloff (crude -20%, Nikkei -10%) where CTAs outperformed equities, then argue AI tools risk crowding (Bloomberg AskB) and overfit backtests via look-ahead bias and 'marking your own homework'; Carver advocates strict add-only backtests, global robust parameters, and diversified trend funds as the default hedge.

insights.claim: If many funds use the same commercial AI (e.g., Bloomberg's AskB) and get the same answers, positions will crowd; crowding hurts relative value and carry trades most, trend following much less.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Expect AI-standardized advice to raise crowding risk in RV/carry books; trend is relatively insulated.
insights.quote: some trades do very badly when they get crowded particularly relative value trades. It's not quite so true with trend following but but certainly carry and relative value definitely do worse if there's crowding

insights.claim: Crowding risk from shared AI tools is concentrated among small-to-midsize hedge funds (e.g., $50M AUM) that cannot build proprietary AI, unlike giants like Goldman Sachs that will have their own.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Smaller-fund flows may become more correlated as they converge on the same vendor AI outputs.

insights.claim: Research described on another podcast found that retail investors given a broker-provided AI were nudged to stop active trading and buy index ETFs, showing AI advice is more persuasive than identical conventional advice — crowding, but in a beneficial direction.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: AI advisers could accelerate retail flows into passive index products.

insights.claim: Position crowding does not require AI: many were long the AI trade and there have been public blowups plus rumored pod blowups; AI may simply make factor crowding worse.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Monitor pod/multi-manager crowding in AI-related factor exposure as a source of unwind risk.

insights.claim: Niels proposed testing whether AskB recommends a common optimal allocation across global equities, global bonds, trend following and gold, on the view that investors may increasingly adopt whatever AI tells them.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: If AI recommendations converge, allocation flows into products like trend following could follow AI defaults.

insights.claim: Crude oil was down about 20% month-to-date in November despite ongoing Middle East tensions and strikes around the Strait of Hormuz, and gold and silver also fell heavily, defying typical safe-haven intuition.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: Geopolitical risk is not translating into energy or precious-metal strength; trend signals favor shorts there.

insights.claim: Nikkei futures were down almost 10% month-to-date in November, with MSCI World down more than 5% (up ~5.25% YTD) and S&P 500 down ~5.25% (up 5.89% YTD).
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: Broad equity drawdown underway in November, with Japan hit hardest.

insights.claim: CTA indices held up better than equities in November: B250 index down ~2.5% MTD/up 10.5% YTD, CTA index down 2.38%/up 11.15%, S10 trend index down 2.87%/up 11.12%, short-term traders index down 8bp/up 5%.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: Trend followers are outperforming equities YTD and limiting losses during the selloff — no crisis yet, so no crisis alpha expected.

insights.claim: Niels's trend barometer read a strong 55, largely driven by trends in energy markets and to some extent equities, suggesting improving conditions for trend followers into late November.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: A strong barometer reading is a forward-looking sign of trend-following opportunity.

insights.claim: Rob Carver's system is at a new high-water mark, up about 13.6% YTD, because as a ~60% trend follower he underperforms in strong trend years and outperforms in weak ones.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Blending trend with other signals smooths results relative to pure trend indices.
insights.quote: I'm up about 13.6% for the year

insights.claim: Rob Carver's largest risk positions are in metals, agriculturals, FX and a bond spread: long Canadian 10-year bonds vs short US 10-year bonds (the 'Carney-Trump trade'), short CHF/USD exposure, and short platinum and silver.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Systematic signals currently favor Canada over US duration and short precious metals.
insights.quote: I'm long Canadian 10-year bonds and short US 10-year bonds

insights.claim: Rob Carver attributes recent outperformance to a diversified set of small, unrelated bets rather than one big macro factor; CTA portfolios, being bottom-up, often end up accidentally concentrated in a single factor such as long equities.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Check whether a CTA's book is concentrated in one factor; diversified books are less exposed to single-factor reversals.

insights.claim: Eckhardt Trading, the firm of Turtle mentor Bill Eckhardt and one of the longest-running futures firms, stopped trading after AUM fell to very low levels, partly due to weak returns in recent years — not a blowup.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: Legacy CTA attrition after poor years shows AUM consolidation pressure in managed futures.

insights.claim: CalPERS, which exited hedge funds more than 10 years ago, said it is returning to hedge funds, possibly under a total portfolio approach that could favor systematic/trend strategies.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: A large pension re-entering hedge funds could signal renewed institutional demand, including for CTAs.

insights.claim: The With Intelligence fund-of-hedge-funds billion-dollar club saw AUM rise more than 10% in the first 6 months of the year to almost $700 billion.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: Fund-of-funds channel is recovering after its post-2008 decline.

insights.claim: Anthropic's first trading day valued it around $1.5 trillion; it closed up about 14% but faded into the close while all major indices fell meaningfully that day.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: Mega AI IPO coincided with broad index weakness — watch for supply/sentiment effects on AI equities.
insights.quote: I think they valued at the end around 1.5 trillion

insights.claim: Rob Carver sarcastically catalogued Tesla's Cybercab launch as falling short of years of robotaxi promises: owners must pay a subscription or the car is bricked, a geofenced area smaller than existing self-driving, two seats, high insurance, NHTSA investigating its certification, and terms banning use as a money-earning taxi.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Skepticism on Tesla's robotaxi economics: the product does not deliver the promised owner-income network.
insights.quote: you can't actually use it as a taxi to earn money from because that's not allowed in the terms and conditions

insights.claim: Niels reported California banned Waymo vehicles from highways after too many incidents, indicating autonomous driving is still a developing technology.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: Regulatory friction remains a headwind for autonomous-vehicle rollout timelines.

insights.claim: For holding periods of about a month or more, continually tweaking one algorithm is at best marginally additive and at worst overfitting; Rob Carver has recalibrated his own system only about twice in 12 years against a backtest back to 1970.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Frequent retuning of slow strategies is a red flag for overfitting in managers or one's own process.

insights.claim: Continuous refitting is appropriate for high-frequency trading because HFT generates thousands of data points a day and suffers faster alpha decay.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Refit cadence should match data density and decay speed of the strategy.

insights.claim: 'Methodology shopping' — trying many fitting/optimization approaches and picking the best in-sample — is itself a meta-level form of in-sample fitting.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Discount backtests from researchers who iterate over optimization methods.
insights.quote: methodology shopping where you basically hunt out the best sort of fitting strategy that gives you the highest performance sort of in sample

insights.claim: Niels argued research still matters: genuinely new, complementary ideas are worthwhile, whereas parameter tweaks to the same methodology are not.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: Judge research departments by new diversifying ideas, not parameter churn.

insights.claim: A Resolve Asset Management paper on idiosyncratic market effects in time-series momentum (50 futures, 1950-2026) found per-market nonlinear response curves fitted pre-1995 gave a small but significant out-of-sample improvement over ~30 years.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Market-specific nonlinear sizing has measurable but modest edge.

insights.claim: Response curves differ by momentum speed: slow momentum is near linear, while fast momentum shows S-shaped tails where very strong trends can mean revert; Carver uses a linear response capped at extremes.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Cap position size on extreme fast-momentum signals to avoid tail mean reversion.

insights.claim: Rob Carver would not implement per-market nonlinear fits because the gain is small relative to the complexity and simple in-sample/out-of-sample splits cannot detect evolving curve shapes.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Prefer robust global models; treat small per-market gains skeptically.

insights.claim: Both Niels's firm (moving from per-market settings to global settings over the last 20 years) and AHL (moving to a robust global setting around 2011) shifted toward simpler global parameters for robustness.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: Industry best practice among leading CTAs favors global, robust parameters over per-market fitting.

insights.claim: Rejecting a tested strategy idea before adding it to the backtest is itself in-sample fitting, because it uses information unavailable at the backtest's start; Carver advocates an 'add-on' backtest where ideas can be added but never deleted (only down-weighted).
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Backtest performance of most strategies is inflated by discarded ideas — haircut reported Sharpe accordingly.
insights.quote: You can only add new ideas to it. Uh you can't delete once.

themes.theme: Limits and uses of AI in strategy design

insights.claim: Rob Carver argues AI cannot generate genuinely original trading ideas, but can surface papers and prompt human ideas, akin to browsing library shelves — while hallucinating references that must be checked.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Use LLMs for literature discovery, not alpha generation.
insights.quote: if you're going to be relying on AI to come up with original ideas, then you know, you might you might end up picking up an idea from elsewhere you weren't aware of, but it isn't going to be an it's not going to be come up with genuinely original ideas

insights.claim: LLM-based backtests (e.g., the 'self-driving portfolio' agentic asset-allocation paper) suffer look-ahead bias because commercial LLMs are trained on data up to their cutoff, and nobody yet refits LLM weights each year as a proper walk-forward test would require.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Treat AI-agent portfolio backtests as contaminated by data leakage until proven otherwise.

insights.claim: Using an LLM both to build a strategy and to judge whether it works, including writing its own backtest code, is 'marking your own homework'.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Demand independent, human-written backtest frameworks when evaluating AI-built strategies.
insights.quote: I call it marking your own homework

insights.claim: AI is useful for idea prompting, summarizing research, finding data sources, writing small (~50-line) verifiable non-core code, and suggesting bugs — in one case 3 of 4 AI code suggestions were good but the 4th would have destroyed the code.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Keep AI out of core execution code and never let AI write and check code unsupervised.

insights.claim: To counter AI's forward-looking knowledge, a backtest of trend following should simultaneously test the opposite hypothesis (mean reversion) because in 1970 you would not have known trend worked.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Robust research tests competing hypotheses side by side to neutralize hindsight embedded in AI or researchers.

insights.claim: Carver says the standard strategy-design loop (economic rationale, signal design, parameter selection, statistical validation, portfolio integration) is how nearly everyone works, and AI will make its embedded in-sample selection problem worse; his book after the one due December 1 will cover strict backtesting.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Expect more overfit AI-assisted strategies; rigor in backtest design becomes a differentiator.

insights.claim: In a linear correlation framework, adding trend following in the same asset class you already hold (e.g., equity trend on an equity-heavy portfolio) adds beta, since trend has positive beta to assets that rise over time; you'd prefer a CTA with less allocation to that asset class.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: An equity-heavy investor should seek CTAs underweight equity trend, not overweight it.

insights.claim: Trend following's tail-hedge splits into a guaranteed mechanical component (going short a falling market) and an empirical 'crisis alpha' component that is not guaranteed — e.g., 2008's protracted selloff was ideal while last year's tariff tantrum sharp drop-and-reversal was awful for medium-speed trend.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Don't count on crisis alpha in V-shaped crashes; it works best in protracted selloffs.

insights.claim: Regardless of the underlying portfolio, investors are probably better off buying a diversified trend-following fund across all asset classes rather than one matching their concentrated exposure.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Allocate to diversified CTAs as the default hedge for any portfolio.
insights.quote: irrespective of what your underlying portfolio is you're probably better off buying just a diversified trend following fund that allocates across all asset classes

insights.claim: Niels cited research (possibly Alex Grman at ISAM) that during equity crises the most consistently profitable CTA sectors are commodities, not the crisis sector — e.g., CTAs got short energies about a month before the 'co' (COVID-era) equity collapse, and positioned in energy before this year's March 1 war start.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: Commodity trend exposure is a key driver of CTA crisis performance; avoid CTAs without broad commodity coverage.

insights.claim: For equity hedging via trend, a 20% allocation is too small to hedge; bonds can be hedged more efficiently because bond trend portfolios can be levered up.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Size trend allocations larger than 20% if the goal is a real equity hedge.

insights.claim: Without futures access, leveraged ETFs (e.g., 2x bond ETFs) are a crude substitute for trend exposure in equities and bonds, but suffer higher cost and daily-reset issues; futures are better for larger accounts.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Retail trend implementers should prefer futures where possible.
